strengths: The paper tackles an important and underexplored problem: making retrosynthesis prediction interpretable through natural-language reasoning grounded in chemical logic, rather than pure pattern matching.

The proposed architecture is a reasonable and well-motivated design: constructing a multi-dimensional 'chemical decision space' from specialized models (reaction type, reaction center, reactant candidates) to ground an LLM's reasoning, combined with a multi-stage rule-based reward (KGPO) that supervises both the reasoning process and the final answer rather than outcome alone.

The empirical evaluation is broad: USPTO-50K, USPTO-FULL, an out-of-distribution ChemBench benchmark, and multi-step retrosynthesis on PaRoutes, with consistent gains over both LLM-based and non-LLM specialized baselines.

The model-agnostic/plug-and-play property (any specialized model can supply candidates without LLM retraining) is empirically demonstrated in Table 2, and performance scales with the quality of the underlying specialized model, supporting the claimed generalization.

Wet-lab validation of two model-proposed synthetic routes (including a first-ever reported synthesis confirmed via SciFinder) is a rare and valuable form of evidence for a chemistry ML paper and substantially strengthens the practical relevance claim.

Interpretability is assessed with both automatic (GPT-4o) and human expert scoring across three well-defined criteria, and ablations (SFT vs GRPO vs KGPO) show KGPO improves both prediction accuracy and reasoning quality, supporting the core design motivation of 'right for the right reasons.'
The reward-hacking analysis (candidate position shuffling) is a thoughtful and empirically validated engineering detail that improves credibility of the RL training methodology.
weaknesses: The rule-based reward for 'reasoning correctness' on sub-tasks (r_i in Eq. 5) is not concretely specified—how is it automatically determined that the generated reasoning text 'contains correct information' for a sub-task (e.g., matching a reaction type string, verifying a reaction-center span in free text)? This is central to the method's claimed novelty (process-level supervision) but is underspecified, harming reproducibility.

Table 6 shows that providing only reactant candidates (no type/center context) yields just 29.1% Top-1 accuracy under KGPO training—substantially below the standalone specialized model's own accuracy (~63–70% for GraphRetro/Graph2Edits). This counter-intuitive drop (the LLM performing far worse than trivially copying the specialized model's top prediction) is not discussed or explained, raising concerns about training dynamics (e.g., the position-shuffling reward-hacking mitigation may remove informative signal when no auxiliary context is present) and casting some doubt on how much of the model's headline gains are attributable to reasoning versus the added context.

The overall accuracy gain over the best pure specialized model is comparatively modest (e.g., 70.3% vs 67.2% Top-1 on USPTO-50K using Graph2Edits candidates), and the self-correction/generation mechanism—highlighted as an 'emergent capability'—only succeeds in 40.6% of the small subset of cases where all candidates are wrong, contributing a small fraction of the overall improvement; the paper's framing risks overstating the significance of the LLM's added reasoning value beyond a strong selection/repair mechanism over already high-quality candidates.

The claim of being 'the first retrosynthesis model capable of generating natural language interpretable reasoning processes' is a strong claim that is not fully reconciled with related work discussed in Section 2 (e.g., LLM+tool integration papers), and could be softened or better substantiated relative to prior LLM-based chemical reasoning efforts.

Wet-lab validation, while a valuable strength, is based on only two hand-picked examples with no baseline comparison (e.g., whether a strong specialized model or vanilla LLM could propose the same or comparable routes), limiting how strongly this evidence generalizes to support broad claims of 'genuine chemical discovery' capability.

Reported results rely on a single backbone LLM (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) and appear to be single-run numbers without variance/error bars, which is a concern given the well-known instability of RL training (GRPO/KGPO) and limits confidence in the precision of the reported gains.

The interpretability human/GPT-4o evaluation (Table 5) compares only against the Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct baseline, not against the stronger general LLMs (GPT-4o, Gemini) or chemistry LLMs shown in Table 1, weakening the comprehensiveness of the interpretability comparison relative to the strongest competing systems.

strengths: The core idea of combining specialized retrosynthesis models (as a 'chemical decision space') with LLM reasoning trained via RL to produce natural-language rationales is a reasonable and relatively novel direction for addressing the black-box nature of retrosynthesis prediction.

When compared on equal footing (Table 2, same specialized model supplying candidates), Retro-Expert does yield a consistent, if modest, improvement over the underlying specialized model alone (e.g., +3.1 points Top-1 over Graph2Edits, +2.8 over UAlign), suggesting the collaborative reasoning does add some value beyond simple candidate selection.

The paper includes an unusually broad set of experiments: USPTO-50K, USPTO-FULL, an OOD ChemBench evaluation, multi-step retrosynthesis on PaRoutes, human + automatic interpretability scoring, and two wet-lab synthesis validations, which is commendable breadth for a single paper.

Ablation studies (decision-space composition, training policy comparison, reward-hacking mitigation, N-candidate sensitivity) are reasonably thorough and the appendix provides extensive qualitative reasoning traces, including failure cases, which aids transparency about where the method struggles.
weaknesses: The headline comparison in Table 1 is misleading: 'Ours' and general LLMs are given a decision space (Top-4 candidates plus knowledge anchors) constructed by a specialized model that itself already achieves 63.9–67.2% Top-1 accuracy (Table 2), while the compared baselines (T5Chem, ChemFormer, nach0, and most chemistry LLMs) are not given this crutch. The reported '26.64% Top-1 improvement' therefore largely reflects the quality of the upstream specialized model's candidate generation rather than genuine LLM reasoning gains; the fairer comparison is Table 2, where the improvement over the same specialized model shrinks to only ~3 points.

Ablation Table 6 corroborates this: providing only reactant candidates (no type/center) already yields 29.1%, and adding center+reactant jumps to 56.7% — numbers that track closely with the specialized model's own accuracy — indicating that most of the performance gain comes from information availability (candidate quality) rather than the LLM's reasoning process, which undercuts the central claim that RL-based reasoning is the primary driver of accuracy.

The 'emergent self-reflection' claim (40.6% success rate when all candidates are wrong) is reported without sample size, confidence intervals, or robustness checks, and Figure 3 contains unremoved Chinese annotation text ('此时候选全错'), suggesting insufficient quality control and raising doubts about how carefully this statistic was validated.

The OOD ChemBench evaluation (Table 4) reduces to a 4-way multiple-choice task with one ground truth and three distractors; general LLMs near chance (~29-33%) while the fine-tuned 'Ours' model scores 57%. Since the model was explicitly RL-trained on this exact candidate-selection/justification format, the gap likely reflects task/format familiarity rather than superior chemical generalization, and no ablation isolates format advantage from genuine reasoning improvement.

The wet-lab validation (n=2 reactions) is too small to support the paper's strong claims of being 'a genuine engine for chemical discovery' or providing 'compelling proof' of practical utility; both reactions are well-precedented transformation types (Suzuki coupling, Jones oxidation) with moderate yields, and no negative/failed attempts are reported, raising concerns about selective reporting.

Interpretability evaluation (Table 5) compares against only an untuned Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct baseline rather than ablated variants (e.g., SFT-only, or GRPO without stage rewards) prompted similarly, making it hard to isolate how much of the explanation-quality improvement is attributable to KGPO specifically versus simply having access to the decision-space context.

The generated reasoning explanations are produced by an LLM post-hoc selecting among candidates proposed by separate black-box specialized models; the paper does not verify faithfulness (i.e., whether the stated rationale genuinely reflects the computational process that produced the final answer), which is a central concern for any interpretability claim and is not addressed.

Minor presentation issues: inconsistent algorithm naming (GRPO vs 'GPRO' in the appendix), reliance on GPT-4o as both an evaluator and implicitly as a comparison point creates potential circularity, and some figures/text appear insufficiently proofread (leftover non-English annotations).

strengths: Novel and well-motivated framework that combines specialized retrosynthesis models (for high-recall candidate/anchor generation) with LLM reasoning trained via RL, directly targeting the long-standing interpretability gap in retrosynthesis prediction.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning single-step (USPTO-50K, USPTO-FULL), multi-step (PaRoutes), and out-of-distribution (ChemBench) settings, with consistent and large improvements over both LLM-based and non-LLM-based baselines.

The paper goes beyond in-silico evaluation and includes wet-lab validation of two model-proposed synthetic routes (one of which is apparently a first-ever reported synthesis), which is a compelling and unusual form of evidence for an ML paper and substantially strengthens the practical significance claim.

Thoughtful ablations isolate the contribution of the decision space components (reaction type/center/reactant) and compare SFT vs. GRPO vs. the proposed KGPO, showing both accuracy and interpretability-quality improvements attributable to the proposed reward design.

Explicit treatment of reward hacking (candidate position shuffling) with supporting analysis (Figure 10), and model-agnostic/plug-and-play claims are tested across multiple specialized-model backbones (Table 2).

Interpretability is evaluated with both automatic (GPT-4o) and human expert scoring across three well-defined criteria, rather than relying solely on qualitative case studies, and extensive qualitative examples (success/failure cases) are provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The comparison against general LLM baselines (GPT-4o, Gemini, Qwen, etc.) is somewhat apples-to-oranges: these baselines are evaluated zero/few-shot on the same decision space without any task-specific RL/SFT training, while Retro-Expert is specifically optimized on the task; the gains could partly reflect the advantage of any fine-tuning over prompting rather than a unique benefit of the proposed collaborative-reasoning architecture. A fine-tuned (SFT or vanilla GRPO) baseline on the same decision space is shown in Table 7, but this ablation is not consistently cross-referenced with Table 1's broader LLM comparisons.

The wet-lab validation, while a nice addition, consists of only two examples with no reporting of failure rate among other candidate novel routes proposed by the model; this is anecdotal rather than statistically robust evidence of 'genuine chemical discovery' capability, and the strong claims in Section 4.5 and the abstract may overstate what two successful cases can support.

The method's accuracy is fundamentally bounded by the upstream specialized models supplying the decision space (explicitly acknowledged as 'performance scales with specialized model accuracy'), raising the question of how much of the LLM's 'reasoning' is actually doing non-trivial work versus selecting among already-filtered high-quality options; the self-correction/generation statistic (40.6% success when all candidates are wrong) is suggestive but could partly reflect the base LLM's pretrained chemical knowledge rather than an emergent capability induced by KGPO specifically (no ablation isolates this).

Training data curation (stratified subsampling to 9k/80k examples from the full datasets) could introduce distributional bias relative to the standard test splits used for comparison with baselines trained on the full datasets; the paper does not discuss how this subsampling affects fairness of comparison with non-LLM baselines trained on the complete training sets.

The GRPO-based objective in Eq. (4) is described generically and does not clearly show the group-relative advantage normalization that defines GRPO, which is a minor technical imprecision; implementation details (e.g., group size, exact advantage computation) are not specified in the main text.

Human evaluation involved only three evaluators with no reported inter-rater agreement or statistical testing, and the untranslated Chinese annotation remaining in Figure 3 suggests incomplete proofreading/editing of the submission.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: prompts and hyperparameters are given in the appendix, but no mention of code or trained model release is made, and the plug-and-play claim across different specialized models (Table 2) is not fully explained regarding whether any adaptation is needed when swapping the specialized model used at inference time versus training time.

strengths: Rare and compelling wet-lab validation: the authors actually synthesized two predicted compounds (a first-ever reported route and a novel alternative route), confirmed by NMR, providing strong real-world evidence beyond typical in-silico benchmarks.

Comprehensive human evaluation protocol with three chemistry PhD annotators, including detailed inter-annotator agreement analysis (Table 13) and fine-grained breakdown of reasoning faithfulness (Table 14), which adds credibility to the interpretability claims.

Thorough and well-designed ablation studies that isolate the individual contributions of the reward model components (Chem-RM) and the KGPO rectified-advantage optimization versus standard GRPO (Tables 7, 8, 16), demonstrating the necessity of each design choice.

Broad experimental coverage across single-step (USPTO-50K/FULL), out-of-distribution (ChemBench), and multi-step (PaRoutes) retrosynthesis settings, along with strong performance gains over both LLM-based and non-LLM-based baselines.
Careful engineering diagnosis and mitigation of reward hacking (candidate position shuffling), supported by empirical positional-distribution analysis (Figure 10), showing methodological rigor.

The core idea—using pure RL over a chemically-grounded decision space derived from specialized models instead of SFT-based imitation—is a reasonably novel and well-motivated alternative to prevailing SFT+RL pipelines for scientific reasoning tasks.
Extensive appendix materials (prompts, training details, failure case analysis, behavior statistics) support reproducibility of the described pipeline.
weaknesses: The framework's 'interpretability' still ultimately depends on outputs from black-box specialized models (T5Chem, GraphRetro, etc.) to construct the decision space; the LLM reasons over these opaque predictions, which somewhat tempers the claim of moving beyond black-box mechanisms.

The overall human-judged 'fully correct reasoning' criterion (all six dimensions correct) only reaches 59% three-annotator agreement, indicating substantial subjectivity/disagreement in reasoning correctness judgments that is not fully reconciled with the headline 82.85% correctness figure reported for correct-answer cases.

Wet-lab validation, while a strong qualitative strength, is based on only two curated cases selected partly for feasibility and novelty, limiting how much can be generalized about practical reliability across the broader chemical space.

The pipeline involves many moving parts and hyperparameters (multiple specialized models, stratified data curation, reward coefficients λ1/λ2/λ3, γ, β, candidate shuffling ratios), which raises concerns about engineering complexity and the ease of independent reproduction/replication by other groups.

Some baseline result rows appear identical or duplicated (e.g., nach0 and ChemCrow(+nach0) report exactly the same numbers in Table 1), which is not clearly explained and raises questions about experimental setup transparency.

The OOD generalization evaluation (ChemBench) is framed as a 4-option multiple-choice task rather than open-ended generation, which is an easier setting than free-form retrosynthesis prediction and may overstate the model's true generalization ability.

Experiments and reasoning fidelity are restricted to a 7B backbone, and the authors acknowledge (in Limitations) that local chemical/mechanistic errors can still occur even when final answers are correct, somewhat qualifying the strength of the interpretability claims made in the main text.

strengths: The paper tackles a genuinely important problem—interpretability in retrosynthesis prediction—and proposes a reasonable architectural idea of combining specialized-model-derived 'decision spaces' with LLM reasoning optimized via RL rather than SFT.

The empirical scope is unusually broad: single-step (USPTO-50K/FULL), multi-step (PaRoutes), OOD generalization (ChemBench), ablations on reward components and candidate space composition, human expert evaluation of reasoning quality, and even wet-lab validation of two predicted routes.

The training-free, tool-grounded 'Chem-RM' reward design (using RDKit for structural/consistency checks) is a sensible alternative to noisy LLM-as-judge or purely outcome-based rewards, and the reward-hacking mitigation via candidate position shuffling (Appendix E) shows some methodological care.
Appendix analyses of candidate-grounded behavior, rejection/self-correction rates, and decision consistency provide useful transparency into what the trained policy is actually doing.
weaknesses: Confounded comparison with LLM baselines: Table 1 shows that simply handing general LLMs the same Top-4 candidate + knowledge-anchor 'space' used by Retro-Expert already boosts accuracy by 20-50 points (e.g., GPT-4o: 0.30%→32.85%, Claude-3.7: 5.73%→55.70%), yet the paper attributes almost all of Retro-Expert's final 75.69% to its RL-trained 'reasoning' rather than to the candidate-space injection itself. The genuine marginal contribution of KGPO over this already-boosted baseline (e.g., Table 8: RL(GRPO) 66.8% vs RL(KGPO) 75.7%, a ~9-point gain under the same space) is comparatively modest, undermining the central narrative that the method represents a breakthrough in 'logical chemical reasoning' versus largely being an LLM-based re-ranker/corrector over a candidate pool whose Top-4 recall is already high.

Table 2's comparisons (Ours(Graph2Edits), Ours(LocalRetro), etc.) similarly risk conflating 'selecting among the specialized model's own high-recall candidate list' with independently discovering reactants; because Top-4/5/10 recall of the underlying small models is already large, the ceiling for improvement via selection/correction is partly set by the small model, not purely by Retro-Expert's reasoning.

Human evaluation reliability is weak for the key reliability claim: 'Overall Correct Reasoning' achieves only 59% 3/3 and 63% 2/3 inter-annotator agreement (Table 13), indicating substantial subjectivity/noise in the central reasoning-correctness metric that the paper otherwise treats as a strong, headline result (82.85% vs 33.60% in Table 5/12).

Explanation-quality evaluation partly relies on GPT-4o scoring outputs from an LLM-based pipeline without reporting correlation/calibration between automatic and human scores, raising self-evaluation bias concerns.

The wet-lab validation, while a nice touch, consists of only two cases and is presented with strong claims ('compelling proof that Retro-Expert is an effective tool for practical chemical discovery'); this is anecdotal and cannot support such a strong generalization claim about reliability of novel route discovery.

The reaction-type/reaction-center component of Chem-RM (Eq. 4) directly uses ground-truth labels for reward computation, which is essentially label-supervised reward dressed as a 'process' reward; moreover, this component cannot be used on USPTO-FULL (no reaction-type labels per Appendix A.1), questioning the generality of the proposed reward framework beyond the curated USPTO-50K subset.

Key design choices (λ1=1.5, λ2=2.0, λ3=1.0, Top-4 candidates, 9k/80k curated training subsets via stratified sampling) are set without principled justification or sensitivity analysis beyond a narrow ablation grid, raising reproducibility and robustness concerns.

Potential data leakage/overlap is not addressed: the specialized models used to build the decision space are themselves trained on the same USPTO splits as the LLM policy and test set, which could inflate apparent 'collaborative' gains.

Overall framing and conclusion statements (e.g., 'a significant step toward trustworthy, collaborative AI for chemical discovery') overreach relative to the evidence provided, especially given the confounds above.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important gap: existing retrosynthesis models (both specialized ML and LLM-SFT based) are black-box or imitation-pattern limited; the paper's goal of pairing specialized chemical knowledge with LLM reasoning for interpretable predictions is well-motivated.

Very broad and multi-faceted empirical evaluation: single-step (USPTO-50K, USPTO-FULL), out-of-distribution generalization (ChemBench), multi-step retrosynthesis (PaRoutes), and even physical wet-lab validation of two predicted synthetic routes with NMR characterization — this breadth is uncommon and strengthens practical credibility.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contributions of the reward model components (rstruct/rreact/rbase), the KGPO rectified advantage vs. standard GRPO, the necessity of the multi-dimensional decision space, and the sensitivity to candidate set size N — these ablations make the design choices well supported.

Human evaluation involving multiple chemistry PhD experts for both reasoning-correctness and explanation-quality (MA/FC/LC) scoring, together with reported inter-annotator agreement and fine-grained breakdowns, adds rigor beyond typical LLM-as-judge-only evaluation.
The paper identifies and empirically addresses a concrete failure mode (positional reward hacking from biased Top-N candidate ordering) via a shuffling strategy, showing methodological care.

Model-agnostic, plug-and-play compatibility with different specialized models (Table 2) is a useful practical property, and the self-reflection/self-correction behavior analysis (43.1% success rate when all candidates are wrong) is an interesting and partially validated claim.
weaknesses: The 'pure RL' framing is somewhat overstated: the chemical decision space the LLM reasons over is produced by specialized models (T5Chem, GraphRetro, etc.) that were themselves trained with full supervision on the same reaction corpora. Thus the pipeline is not free of supervised pattern-matching; it is displaced into the upstream specialized models, which weakens the contrast drawn with SFT-based LLM baselines in the introduction and Figure 1.

In Table 1, simply providing the chemical decision space to off-the-shelf closed-source LLMs (no RL) already yields large jumps (e.g., Claude-3-7-sonnet reaches 55.7% Top-1, Gemini-2.5-Pro 50.6%) which narrows the gap to the proposed method (75.7%) considerably; the paper does not fully disentangle how much of the final performance is attributable to decision-space construction versus the KGPO optimization itself, beyond the single SFT-vs-KGPO comparison.

The reward model (Chem-RM) components rely on heuristic substructure overlap (RDKit-based) and ground-truth candidate labels (rreact uses c_i^gt directly), which makes the reward partially dependent on having access to gold intermediate labels at training time; the degree to which this generalizes to products/reaction types without such granular annotations is not deeply examined.

Wet-lab validation, while a valuable addition, is limited to two hand-selected Top-1 cases chosen explicitly for novelty/feasibility/diversity; this is a very small and non-random sample that cannot support strong generalizable claims about practical discovery utility, and no failure cases or baseline comparisons are reported in the wet-lab section.

Human-evaluation inter-annotator agreement for the central 'Overall Correct Reasoning' judgment is relatively low (59% unanimous, 63% majority) compared to other sub-dimensions, suggesting non-trivial annotation noise in the key reliability metric reported in Table 5/12.

The multi-step retrosynthesis extension (Section 4.7) is comparatively underdeveloped: route-level search is fully delegated to an existing specialized multi-step model (DMS-Model) with the LLM only re-ranking/adjusting Top-4 routes in a single pass, so the contribution here is more incremental and the comparison table (success rate, Top-K, inference time) lacks detail on how beam size and route-space construction affect fairness versus MCTS/Retro* baselines.

Presentation issues: several references carry implausible future publication years (e.g., 2026 for Nature Chemistry, ICLR, Su et al.) which, whether a formatting artifact or not, should be corrected; dense notation in the problem formulation (Section 3.2) and reward equations could be streamlined for clarity.

No discussion of the added inference-time/computational cost of running multiple specialized models plus an LLM reasoning pass per prediction relative to single-model baselines, which is relevant for practical deployment claims.
